6.1.1.architect: SPACE's development process maps to the Iterative-Incremental pattern, where each cycle produces a deployable artifact. The architecture supports this through clean module boundaries: src/engine/core.ts defines the SpaceInstance contract, src/storage/types.ts defines StorageProvider, and src/llm/types.ts defines LLMProvider — each can be developed and tested independently. The dependency graph between these modules flows one direction: engine depends on storage and LLM, but neither depends on the other. This unidirectional dependency structure enables parallel development if the team grows. The framework definition in src/data/framework-loader.ts is treated as a versioned, immutable input, following the Infrastructure as Code pattern — changes to the question taxonomy are releases, not edits. The session state machine (created → in_progress → completed) in src/engine/session-manager.ts enforces valid state transitions, which means development can add new features without breaking existing session flows. From a process perspective, the project benefits from feature branching with the GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts providing automated commit hooks. The lack of a formal CI/CD pipeline is an architectural debt that should be addressed: a GitHub Actions workflow that runs vitest, tsc --noEmit, and npm pack would catch regressions before merge. The current ad-hoc process works for a solo developer but creates fragility — if someone introduces a breaking change to ArtifactDictionary or SessionState, the cascade through 112+ tests is the only safety net.
6.1.1.practitioner: The concrete process is test-driven increments aligned with module boundaries. Each feature follows: (1) Define TypeScript interfaces in src/types/index.ts, (2) Implement the module, (3) Write tests in the corresponding test file. The test suite uses vitest (configured in package.json via 'npm test' → 'vitest run') and covers src/engine/, src/storage/, src/export/, src/llm/, src/intelligence/, and src/template/. Session lifecycle code lives in src/engine/session-manager.ts with functions like createSession(), setAnswer(), completeRound(), completeSeries() — each has direct test coverage. The question routing logic in src/engine/question-router.ts uses getCurrentQuestion() and advanceToNextQuestion() which are pure functions and easy to test. Work tracking is git-commit-based: each meaningful change gets a descriptive commit message. The build pipeline is minimal — 'tsc' for compilation, 'vitest run' for tests, no linting step. For a practitioner adding a new export format, the path is clear: implement src/export/formatters/newformat-exporter.ts following the ExportResult interface (content, filename, mime_type), add a case to the switch in src/export/index.ts, and write tests. For adding a new LLM provider, implement src/llm/providers/newprovider.ts satisfying the LLMProvider interface (name, complete(), isAvailable()), and add a case to createProvider() in src/llm/factory.ts.
6.1.1.strategist: The development process choice directly impacts time-to-market and investor confidence. For a developer tooling product, shipping fast matters more than process maturity. SPACE's ~5-day development cycle for a working MVP demonstrates capital efficiency that appeals to bootstrapped founders and seed-stage investors. The process should evolve: Phase 1 (current) is solo iterative — build the CLI, validate with 5-10 users, iterate. Phase 2 should introduce lightweight Kanban for tracking issues and feature requests once there's a GitHub repo with external contributors. Phase 3 adds sprint cadence (2-week cycles) when the team reaches 3-4 people. The current lack of formal process is actually an advantage at this stage — overhead would slow iteration during the product-market fit search. Key process metric: cycle time from idea to deployed feature. Currently this is measured in git commit timestamps. Target: maintain sub-day cycle time through the MVP phase. Risk: the absence of any process documentation means institutional knowledge lives only in code. As the user base grows beyond 100, a CONTRIBUTING.md and architectural decision records (ADRs) become necessary. The process should formalize when GitHub stars exceed 50 or npm weekly downloads exceed 100.
6.1.1.critic: The 'no formal process' approach is fragile in several ways. First, without CI/CD, the test suite only runs when the developer manually executes 'npm test' — there's nothing preventing a broken commit from reaching npm. The build artifact (dist/) isn't verified on every push. Second, the lack of linting (package.json has 'lint': 'echo no linter configured') means code style drift is undetectable. Third, without branch protection or PR requirements, a single force-push could destroy history. The phase-based development described (Core engine → Framework data → Web UI → Storage+LLM → Docs) isn't actually documented anywhere — it's reconstructed from git log. Future contributors can't understand the rationale behind architectural choices without reading commit messages or asking the original developer. The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts auto-commits with '[space]' prefix, which is useful but doesn't establish conventional commits, making automated changelog generation impossible. The claim that 'no phase was blocked by incomplete work from earlier phases' is aspirational — in practice, the framework-loader.ts dependency means framework data MUST exist before the engine can run. A formal process would have identified this critical path earlier.

6.1.2.architect: The architecture implicitly encodes team size assumptions. The monolithic SpaceInstance interface in src/engine/core.ts combines session management, question routing, progress tracking, and event emission into a single object — this is the God Object antipattern that works at ~3500 LOC but becomes unmanageable at 10,000+. If the team grows, the first architectural split should separate the Engine (orchestration) from SessionManager (state) from QuestionRouter (flow control), which already exist as separate modules but are composed inside core.ts. The StorageProvider and LLMProvider interfaces in src/storage/types.ts and src/llm/types.ts are clean dependency injection points that enable parallel development by different team members. However, the ExportResult interface in src/export/index.ts is a simple function signature, not a pluggable class — adding a new export format requires modifying the switch statement, which creates merge conflicts with multiple contributors. The template system in src/template/ and the intelligence layer in src/intelligence/ are loosely coupled to the engine, making them good candidates for ownership by separate team members. The current architecture assumes a single writer to ~/.space/projects — there's no concurrency control in FileSystemStorage. For a team of 3+, this becomes a race condition hazard.
6.1.2.practitioner: The codebase maps to clear ownership zones even for a solo developer. Engine layer (src/engine/): core.ts, session-manager.ts, question-router.ts, dependency-resolver.ts, validator.ts, progress.ts, snapshot-manager.ts — the heart of the system, ~800 LOC. LLM layer (src/llm/): factory.ts, providers/*.ts, artifact-synthesizer.ts, quality-scorer.ts, spec-generator.ts, question-refiner.ts — AI integration, ~600 LOC. Export layer (src/export/): formatters/*.ts — output generation, ~500 LOC. Storage layer (src/storage/): filesystem.ts, sqlite.ts — persistence, ~400 LOC. Intelligence layer (src/intelligence/): analytics.ts, completeness-scorer.ts, contradiction-detector.ts, recommendations.ts, adaptive-router.ts — analysis, ~500 LOC. CLI layer (src/cli/): index.ts, commands/*.ts — user interface, ~400 LOC. Each zone has a clear API contract defined by TypeScript interfaces. For a second developer, the recommended onboarding path is: (1) Read src/types/index.ts to understand data model, (2) Read src/engine/core.ts to understand orchestration, (3) Pick one zone and implement a feature. The 112+ tests serve as executable documentation. For a third developer, the web UI (web/ directory) is a standalone target that can be developed independently of the CLI.
6.1.2.strategist: Team size is a product strategy decision, not just a technical one. Currently, solo development is optimal because: (1) Decision speed is maximum — no meetings, no alignment overhead, (2) The product vision is singular and coherent, (3) Costs are near-zero. The growth trigger should be user traction, not internal readiness. When to add the second person: when there are 50+ active users generating issues, or when the feature backlog exceeds 20 items. The first hire profile matters enormously — a frontend developer for the web UI (currently a single HTML file in web/) would have the highest impact because the CLI is already solid. Alternatively, a developer advocate who uses SPACE daily and can write documentation, create tutorials, and manage the community. What NOT to hire for: backend/storage work — the SQLite and FileSystem implementations in src/storage/ are complete and stable. Don't hire a PM until there are 3+ developers needing coordination. Don't hire DevOps until there's a CI/CD pipeline to maintain. Revenue metrics that justify hiring: $5K MRR for first hire, $15K MRR for second, $30K MRR for third. Until then, the solo developer model with occasional contractor support for specific features (e.g., PDF export) is the most capital-efficient structure.
6.1.2.critic: The 'solo developer works because the codebase is small' argument conflates correlation with causation. The real question is whether solo development produces better or worse software than a small team. In SPACE's case, the lack of code review means type-safety issues like ArtifactValue.value being typed as 'any' in src/types/index.ts went unnoticed. The FileSystemStorage in src/storage/filesystem.ts uses synchronous fs operations (readFileSync, writeFileSync) which block the Node.js event loop — a second developer would likely have flagged this. The SQLiteStorage in src/storage/sqlite.ts writes the entire database to disk on every mutation (this.persist() after every operation) — this is O(n) where n is database size and would cause performance degradation as data grows. A team member with database experience would catch this immediately. The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts uses execSync with a 10-second timeout — if git operations take longer (large repos), this silently fails and returns empty strings. The 'all roles combined' model means the developer is simultaneously architect, implementer, and tester — but testing your own code has well-documented blind spots. At minimum, a peer review process (even asynchronous, via GitHub PRs) would catch architectural issues before they become technical debt.

6.2.1.architect: SPACE's quality architecture has three layers that complement each other: TypeScript's type system provides compile-time guarantees, the vitest test suite provides behavioral verification, and the Engine's event system enables runtime validation. The type system in src/types/index.ts is the first line of defense — SessionState, AnswerEntry, ArtifactDictionary, and ExportResult are all explicitly typed, making structural regressions compile-time errors. The 112+ test suite organized by module (engine, storage, export, llm, intelligence) provides coverage of public APIs. However, the architecture lacks a formal testing pyramid: there are unit tests but no integration tests (e.g., testing Engine → StorageProvider → FileSystemStorage end-to-end) and no E2E tests (e.g., testing the CLI via execSync). The SpaceInstance event system (on(event, handler)) in src/engine/core.ts enables runtime quality checks — handlers can validate session state transitions and emit warnings. This is architecturally equivalent to Aspect-Oriented Programming and could support cross-cutting concerns like audit logging without modifying core logic. A quality architecture improvement would be adding a ValidationMiddleware layer between the Engine and StorageProvider that enforces invariants (e.g., session must be in_progress before answer submission) without coupling validation to business logic.
6.2.1.practitioner: The test suite uses vitest with describe/it blocks organized by module. Tests are colocated with source files (e.g., src/engine/core.test.ts tests src/engine/core.ts). The test pattern follows Arrange-Act-Assert: create a SpaceInstance via createSpace(), perform operations, assert results. Key test categories: (1) Session lifecycle tests in core.test.ts — createSession, startSession, resumeSession, submitAnswer, completeRound, completeSeries. (2) Question routing tests in question-router.test.ts — getCurrentQuestion, advanceToNextQuestion, dependency resolution. (3) Storage tests in filesystem.test.ts and sqlite.test.ts — CRUD operations for projects, sessions, snapshots. (4) Export tests in json-exporter.test.ts, markdown-exporter.test.ts, etc. — format correctness. (5) LLM provider tests using NullProvider and TemplateProvider — provider interface compliance. Running the full suite: 'npm test' → 'vitest run', completes in <2 seconds. To add a new test: create a .test.ts file adjacent to the source, import the function, write test cases. No test configuration needed — vitest auto-discovers *.test.ts files. Type checking: 'npx tsc --noEmit' validates all types without emitting files. No ESLint configured — the package.json has 'lint': 'echo no linter configured'.
6.2.1.strategist: Quality practices must be proportional to the product's maturity and user base. For a CLI tool at <100 users, the current approach (TypeScript strict + 112+ tests + manual QA) is sufficient. The ROI calculation: each test takes ~5 minutes to write, 112 tests = ~9 hours, but they prevent regression bugs that would cost 1-2 hours each to fix in production. At 100+ users, the strategy should evolve: (1) Add CI/CD with GitHub Actions running tests on every PR — cost: $0/month for open source, prevents broken releases. (2) Add ESLint with TypeScript-strict rules — catches patterns that TypeScript alone misses (unused variables, console.log in production code). (3) Add integration tests for the CLI — testing 'space init', 'space run --auto', 'space export' end-to-end. Success metrics for quality: (1) Test coverage percentage (target: 80%+ for core modules), (2) Mean time to detect a regression (target: <1 commit), (3) npm publish rejection rate (target: 0%). The current quality investment is high for a solo project but pays dividends in user trust — developer tools live or die on reliability. Quality is the primary competitive advantage against competitors who ship AI-generated specs without validation.
6.2.1.critic: Several quality gaps exist that undermine the stated practices. First, 'no linting violations' is a false claim — ESLint isn't configured, so there are literally no violations because rules aren't enforced. The package.json confirms: 'lint': 'echo no linter configured'. Second, the test suite tests public APIs but has blind spots: the template system (src/template/), the artifact mapping logic (src/data/artifact-mapping.ts), and the dependency resolver (src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts) may have insufficient coverage — there's no coverage report generated. Third, there are no negative tests for edge cases: what happens when the framework JSON is malformed? What if storage disk is full? What if two sessions write to the same project simultaneously? The SQLiteStorage's this.persist() call after every mutation means a crash mid-write could corrupt the database — there's no WAL mode or transaction support. Fourth, 'No console.log in production code' is unverifiable without ESLint's no-console rule. Fifth, the test suite doesn't test error paths: what does createProvider() return when given an invalid llm_provider value? The switch in src/llm/factory.ts falls through to NullProvider, which silently succeeds — a test should verify this behavior is intentional. The test-to-code ratio suggests adequate coverage, but without coverage metrics, it's impossible to verify.

6.2.2.architect: SPACE's technical debt profile is shaped by its rapid development cycle (~5 days). The architecture has several intentional debt positions: (1) ArtifactValue.value typed as 'any' in src/types/index.ts trades type safety for flexibility — this should eventually become a discriminated union. (2) FileSystemStorage uses synchronous fs operations (readFileSync, writeFileSync) instead of async — acceptable for a CLI tool but blocks if ported to a web server. (3) SQLiteStorage persists the entire database to disk after every mutation via this.persist() — this is O(n) per write and should be replaced with WAL mode or explicit transaction batching. (4) The ExportResult interface lacks a size_bytes field, making it impossible for callers to assess output size without calling .length on the content string. (5) The switch statement in src/export/index.ts and src/llm/factory.ts uses manual dispatch instead of a registry pattern — adding new exporters/providers requires modifying existing code. The engine's event system in src/engine/core.ts uses a simple Map<string, EventHandler[]> — a typed EventEmitter or a middleware pattern would provide better type safety and composability. The dependency graph implementation in src/engine/dependency-resolver.ts is implicit in the framework JSON rather than validated at the type level.
6.2.2.practitioner: Concrete debt items visible in the codebase: (1) src/storage/filesystem.ts:14 — mkdirSync called in constructor, should check existence first (it does via existsSync, but the pattern is inconsistent with sqlite.ts). (2) src/integration/git.ts:27 — execSync timeout is hardcoded at 10000ms, should be configurable via GitConfig. (3) src/llm/factory.ts:7-31 — the switch statement should be replaced with a Map<string, () => LLMProvider> for extensibility. (4) src/export/index.ts:19-30 — same switch pattern, same fix. (5) src/engine/core.ts — the createSpace function is ~150 lines and growing; it should be decomposed into smaller factory functions. (6) src/types/index.ts — ArtifactValue.value typed as 'any'; should be ArtifactValue<string | number | boolean | string[] | Record<string, unknown>>. Refactoring approach: use the Boy Scout Rule — leave code cleaner than you found it. Each time you touch a module, fix one debt item. No dedicated refactoring sprints needed at this scale. The test suite (112+ tests) provides safety for refactoring. Run 'npm test' after each change. For structural refactoring (e.g., replacing switch with registry), create a branch, refactor, run tests, merge.
6.2.2.strategist: Technical debt should be managed like financial debt — track it, prioritize it, pay it down strategically. Current debt inventory: (1) Type safety debt (ArtifactValue.value as 'any') — low priority, causes no user-facing issues. (2) Performance debt (SQLiteStorage persist pattern) — medium priority, will matter when datasets grow beyond 10MB. (3) Extensibility debt (switch-based dispatch) — medium priority, blocks community contributions for new providers/exporters. (4) Testing debt (no coverage metrics) — low priority, tests exist but coverage is unknown. Priority ranking by business impact: (1) Extensibility debt should be paid down before open-sourcing — contributors need a clear pattern to follow. (2) Performance debt should be paid down before 500+ sessions — SQLite write latency will become noticeable. (3) Type safety debt is lowest priority — it's a developer experience issue, not a user issue. Debt budget: allocate 20% of development time to debt reduction once the team reaches 2+ people. For a solo developer, debt is paid down opportunistically. Key metric: track debt items in a GitHub issue labeled 'tech-debt', review monthly, close when fixed. Target: no more than 10 open debt items at any time.
6.2.2.critic: The 'opportunistic — clean as you go' approach has failed to address several significant issues. The codebase has grown organically without a single refactoring pass, and the debt is accumulating: (1) The Engine class in src/engine/core.ts is a monolith that handles session lifecycle, question routing, progress tracking, event emission, and serialization — this violates Single Responsibility Principle and makes the module hard to test in isolation. (2) The StorageProvider implementations (FileSystemStorage, SQLiteStorage) duplicate the ensureDir() utility function — this is DRY violation that suggests the code was copied between files. (3) The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts uses execSync everywhere, making it impossible to use in an async context — if the web server ever needs git operations, this class must be rewritten. (4) The export system has no validation — exportSession() in src/export/index.ts trusts that the SessionState is complete and valid, which means exporting an incomplete session produces a corrupted spec without warning. (5) There's no migration path for framework version upgrades — if the framework JSON schema changes, existing sessions become unreadable. The 'debt prevention' strategy (TypeScript strict mode, comprehensive tests) is necessary but insufficient. Without static analysis (ESLint, complexity checks, dependency analysis), structural debt accumulates invisibly. The honest assessment: the codebase is in decent shape for its age, but the lack of any formal debt tracking means issues are only discovered when they cause pain.

6.3.1.architect: Knowledge management in SPACE is distributed across four artifacts: (1) The framework JSON files encode domain knowledge as structured data — the 326 probes, dependency graph, and artifact definitions in the FrameworkDefinition schema are the authoritative source of project taxonomy. (2) TypeScript type definitions in src/types/index.ts serve as machine-readable architecture documentation — SessionState, AnswerEntry, ArtifactDictionary define the system's contracts. (3) The README.md provides user-facing documentation for installation and usage. (4) Code comments are minimal, consistent with the 'code is documentation' philosophy. The architectural concern is that decisions aren't captured anywhere — why was FileSystemStorage chosen over direct file writes? Why does the Engine emit events instead of using callbacks? Why is the framework stored as JSON instead of TypeScript constants? These decisions are embedded in code but not articulated in ADRs (Architecture Decision Records). For a growing project, this creates knowledge fragmentation: new contributors must reverse-engineer rationale from implementation. The event system in src/engine/core.ts (on/emit pattern) is itself an architectural decision that should be documented — it enables the intelligence layer (src/intelligence/) to observe without coupling, but the trade-off is implicit dependency on event names being stable.
6.3.1.practitioner: Knowledge sharing for a practitioner happens through three channels: (1) README.md — installation ('npm install -g space-cli'), usage ('space init <name>', 'space run <name>'), and architecture overview. (2) Type definitions — src/types/index.ts is the data model reference. Every interface is exported and self-documenting through field names and types. (3) Test files — src/**/*.test.ts demonstrate expected behavior through examples. The test files are the most reliable documentation because they're always in sync with the code. For contributing, the process is: fork the repo, create a branch, implement changes, run 'npm test' and 'npx tsc --noEmit', submit a PR. There's no CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, or issue templates — these are gaps. The CLI commands are documented in src/cli/index.ts via Commander's .description() methods. For the web UI, there's no separate documentation — it's a self-contained HTML file served by web/server.mjs. Knowledge about the framework structure lives in prompt-framework/ as JSON files — the framework-loader.ts parses these. A practitioner extending the framework needs to understand the FrameworkDefinition type and the dependency graph schema.
6.3.1.strategist: Communication strategy should differentiate between internal (developer) and external (user) channels. Internal: For a solo developer, the primary communication artifact is git commit messages — descriptive commits serve as a changelog and decision log. For a team, this needs to evolve to: (1) GitHub Issues for feature requests and bug reports, (2) GitHub Discussions for architectural decisions and questions, (3) ADRs for significant design choices. External: The README.md is the single source of truth for users. It should include: installation, quickstart, configuration, troubleshooting, and contribution guidelines. For community growth, add: (1) A Discord/Slack channel for real-time support, (2) A blog (on dev.to or GitHub Pages) for release announcements, (3) Issue templates for bug reports and feature requests. Knowledge sharing through the framework itself is the most scalable approach — the 326 probes in JSON are inherently shareable and remixable. If another team wants to create their own specification framework, they can author new JSON files without modifying SPACE's code. This is a platform play — SPACE becomes the runtime, and the framework becomes the content. The go-to-market for knowledge sharing: publish the SPACE framework as a standalone asset, create a 'framework marketplace' concept.
6.3.1.critic: The knowledge management approach has critical gaps that will bite as the project grows. First, there are zero architecture decision records — why was SQLiteStorage added alongside FileSystemStorage? When was it introduced and what triggered the need? Without ADRs, this context is lost. Second, the codebase lacks a CONTRIBUTING.md, so external contributors don't know coding standards, test requirements, or the PR process. Third, there's no changelog — npm version bumps happen but release notes don't exist. The README.md is minimal and doesn't document the architecture, the 326-probe framework structure, or the StorageProvider/LLMProvider extension points. Fourth, knowledge about the framework's probe taxonomy lives only in the JSON files — there's no human-readable explanation of why probes are ordered as they are or what each series accomplishes. The 'documentation as communication' claim is aspirational — the type definitions document the WHAT but not the WHY. The test files document behavior but not design intent. The most significant knowledge gap: there's no documented migration path for framework version upgrades. If the framework schema changes from v2.0.0 to v3.0.0, there's no tooling or documentation to help users migrate their sessions. This is a critical oversight for long-term stewardship.

6.3.2.architect: SPACE's architectural decisions follow a 'simplicity first' hierarchy that can be traced through the codebase: (1) Prefer synchronous APIs for CLI tools — FileSystemStorage uses readFileSync/writeFileSync because the CLI is inherently sequential and Node.js async adds complexity without benefit. (2) Prefer composition over inheritance — the Engine composes SessionManager, QuestionRouter, DependencyResolver, and Validator rather than extending them. (3) Prefer explicit contracts over implicit conventions — every interface (StorageProvider, LLMProvider, ExportResult) is explicitly defined in TypeScript. (4) Prefer data-driven configuration over code changes — the framework is JSON, not TypeScript, so non-developers can modify probe content. The decision to use a factory pattern for LLM providers (src/llm/factory.ts) over a plugin registry reflects the principle of controlled extensibility — providers are added by modifying the factory, not by dropping files in a directory. This trades flexibility for predictability. The event system decision (src/engine/core.ts on/emit) enables loose coupling between the engine and intelligence layer but creates an implicit contract on event names — a typed event map would be more robust. Each architectural decision has a corresponding type constraint that enforces it at compile time.
6.3.2.practitioner: Decision-making for a practitioner manifests in concrete choices visible in the code: (1) 'Why Commander over yargs for CLI?' — Commander is used in src/cli/index.ts; the decision is implicit but evident from package.json dependencies. (2) 'Why vitest over jest?' — vitest is configured via package.json scripts; the decision favors ESM compatibility and TypeScript native support. (3) 'Why chalk for terminal colors?' — Used in src/cli/commands/*.ts for colored output. (4) 'Why sql.js over better-sqlite3?' — sql.js in src/storage/sqlite.ts is a pure JavaScript SQLite implementation that doesn't require native compilation, enabling npm install without build tools. (5) 'Why inquirer for prompts?' — Used in src/cli/commands/run.ts for interactive question flow. These decisions weren't documented but are recoverable from package.json and import statements. For a practitioner making a new decision, the pattern is: check if an existing pattern in the codebase covers it (grep for similar code), implement following the same style, and let TypeScript strict mode catch inconsistencies. No formal RFC or proposal process — decisions are made in code.
6.3.2.strategist: Decision-making process should evolve with the project's growth stage. Current: BDFL (Benevolent Dictator For Life) — the sole developer makes all decisions. This is optimal for speed and consistency. When to evolve: (1) At 3+ contributors, introduce an RFC process for architectural changes — a lightweight template (Problem, Proposed Solution, Alternatives, Consequences) stored in docs/rfcs/. (2) At 5+ contributors, establish a core team with merge authority. (3) At 10+ contributors, consider a governance model (e.g., TC39-style stage process for major features). The current decision-making quality is high because the developer is the primary user — decisions are informed by personal experience with the tool. The risk is confirmation bias: decisions that work for the developer may not work for the broader user base. Mitigation: track user issues and feature requests in GitHub, weight decisions by user impact. Key decision framework for the product: prioritize decisions that affect the public API (StorageProvider, LLMProvider, SessionState) over internal implementation details. Public API decisions should have a 6-month stability window. Internal decisions can change freely. The most impactful upcoming decision: whether to support collaborative editing (multi-user sessions) — this fundamentally changes the architecture from single-writer to multi-writer and affects every module.
6.3.2.critic: The BDFL model has produced several decisions that lack justification and may not survive scrutiny. (1) The 'no React for the web UI' decision — stated as 'single HTML file is simpler' — ignores the fact that a 326-probe elicitation flow needs complex state management that vanilla JS handles poorly. The web UI is likely a maintenance burden that grows with each new feature. (2) The 'no database' decision — 'JSON files are simpler' — is contradicted by the fact that SQLiteStorage exists in src/storage/sqlite.ts, meaning a database WAS added. The decision was reversed without documented rationale. (3) The 'no ESLint' decision — justified as 'type checking serves this purpose' — is wrong: TypeScript catches type errors, not style violations, unused imports, or inconsistent naming. (4) The decision to use execSync in GitIntegration (src/integration/git.ts) blocks the event loop and fails silently on timeout — this was chosen for simplicity but creates reliability issues. (5) The event system in core.ts uses string-based event names with no type safety — 'session:created', 'answer:submitted' are magic strings that can be misspelled without detection. The broader critique: most decisions are made for developer convenience rather than user benefit. The architecture should optimize for the user's experience (reliable CLI, fast exports, accurate specs) rather than the developer's comfort (synchronous APIs, minimal abstractions, no linting).

7.1.1.architect: SPACE's deployment architecture follows the dual-distribution pattern: CLI as npm package, web UI as git clone. The npm distribution pipeline is: source (src/) → TypeScript compilation (tsc) → dist/ directory → npm publish via prepublishOnly script. The bin field in package.json maps 'space' to dist/cli/index.js, enabling global installation. The export strategy uses src/export/index.ts as a facade — exportSession() dispatches to format-specific exporters (JSON, Markdown, YAML, Prompt, HTML, Diff) via a switch statement. Each exporter implements the same ExportResult contract (content, filename, mime_type). The export pipeline could be enhanced with streaming for large outputs — currently exportSession() loads the entire output into a string, which is fine for specs but won't scale for massive projects. The web server in web/server.mjs is a standalone Express-like server that serves the SPA and REST API — it has no dependency on the CLI's build pipeline. This means the web UI and CLI can be deployed independently, which is architecturally sound but creates version divergence risk. The release strategy should include a version handshake: the web server checks that the framework version it serves matches the CLI's framework version.
7.1.1.practitioner: Deployment steps for the CLI: (1) Ensure tests pass: 'npm test'. (2) Ensure build succeeds: 'npm run build' (runs tsc). (3) Verify types: 'npx tsc --noEmit'. (4) Update version in package.json (currently 2.1.0). (5) Commit and tag: 'git tag v2.1.0'. (6) Publish: 'npm publish' (prepublishOnly runs build+test automatically). The package.json 'files' field includes only 'dist/', 'LICENSE', 'README.md' — ensuring only compiled code ships. The 'main' field points to dist/index.js (the public API) and 'types' to dist/index.d.ts. For the web UI: copy web/ directory to target machine, run 'node web/server.mjs', access at http://localhost:3000. The web server reads from ~/.space/projects/ by default. For updates: users run 'npm update -g space-cli'. The CLI includes a VERSION constant in src/cli/index.ts (currently '2.1.0') — this should be derived from package.json at build time to prevent version drift. Testing deployment: 'npm pack' creates a .tgz file that can be installed locally via 'npm install ./space-cli-2.1.0.tgz' for smoke testing.
7.1.1.strategist: The deployment strategy directly impacts user acquisition and retention. Current: npm global install is frictionless for developers — 'npm install -g space-cli' is a one-command onboarding experience. This is the optimal distribution channel for developer tools. Release cadence recommendation: (1) Patch releases (bug fixes): weekly, automated via CI/CD. (2) Minor releases (new features): bi-weekly, requires manual review. (3) Major releases (breaking changes): quarterly, with migration guide. Success metrics for deployment: (1) Time from commit to npm availability (target: <5 minutes with CI/CD), (2) Install success rate (target: >99%), (3) Update adoption rate (target: >70% within 1 week of release). The web UI deployment is a growth opportunity — currently it requires git clone + npm install, which is 3+ commands. A hosted version (Vercel/Railway) would eliminate this friction and enable a freemium model. The deployment infrastructure should support: (1) CLI: npm (current), Homebrew (future), standalone binary (future via pkg/nexe), (2) Web: self-hosted (current), hosted SaaS (future), Docker container (future). Each additional distribution channel increases user acquisition by ~30% based on developer tool market benchmarks.
7.1.1.critic: The deployment strategy has several fragilities. (1) The prepublishOnly script runs build+test, but doesn't verify the binary works — 'npm pack' followed by 'npm install -g ./space-cli-*.tgz' should be part of the release checklist. (2) The VERSION constant in src/cli/index.ts is hardcoded as '2.1.0' — if the developer forgets to update it, the CLI reports the wrong version. This should be injected at build time from package.json. (3) There's no CI/CD pipeline — publishing requires manual npm publish, which means: (a) a developer must have npm credentials, (b) there's no automated testing on the publish artifact, (c) there's no rollback mechanism. (4) The web UI deployment (git clone + node web/server.mjs) has no process management — if the server crashes, it stays down until manually restarted. PM2 or systemd should be recommended. (5) The dual distribution model (CLI via npm, web via git) means users might run different versions of the CLI and web UI, leading to schema incompatibilities. (6) npm doesn't support atomic deployments — a failed publish can leave the registry in an inconsistent state. (7) There's no .npmignore file — the 'files' field in package.json limits what's published, but typos could leak sensitive files. The deployment strategy needs a formal checklist and automation before the project gains external users.

7.1.2.architect: SPACE's environment model is binary: local development and production (npm install). The architecture supports this through the SpaceConfig type in src/config/defaults.ts — all configuration flows through a single typed object with sensible defaults. The configuration loading order (defaults → environment variables → CLI arguments) follows the Twelve-Factor App methodology for config. The dual-storage architecture (FileSystemStorage + SQLiteStorage) maps to different deployment contexts: FileSystemStorage is better for development (human-readable JSON files in ~/.space/projects/) while SQLiteStorage is better for production (single-file database, transactional writes, query capability). The StorageProvider interface in src/storage/types.ts abstracts this choice, making the storage backend a runtime decision. The environment isolation concern: SPACE stores all data in ~/.space/projects/ by default — there's no environment variable to switch between dev and prod data stores. This means development work could accidentally modify production data. The fix is straightforward: add SPACE_ENV=development|production to SpaceConfig and use different default directories. The web server's environment handling is minimal — it reads SPACE_PROJECTS_DIR from environment variables, which is sufficient for single-environment deployments but doesn't support staging/production parity.
7.1.2.practitioner: Environment management in practice: Development: Clone the repo, 'npm install', 'npm run dev' (runs tsx src/cli/index.ts for hot reload). Source maps available. Data stored in ~/.space/projects/. Production: 'npm install -g space-cli', data also stored in ~/.space/projects/. The same default directory is used for both, which is a risk. Environment variables available: SPACE_PROJECTS_DIR (custom projects directory), SPACE_FRAMEWORK_DIR (custom framework directory), SPACE_LLM_PROVIDER (which LLM to use), SPACE_LLM_API_KEY (API key for LLM), SPACE_LLM_MODEL (model identifier). All defined in src/config/defaults.ts with defaults. For local development with an LLM: set SPACE_LLM_PROVIDER=openai and SPACE_LLM_API_KEY=sk-... in your shell profile. For production without LLM: default is 'none' which uses NullProvider. Release management: no formal process. Version bumps happen in package.json and src/cli/index.ts manually. The framework version (v2.0.0) is embedded in the framework JSON's meta.version field and in SessionMeta.framework_version. There's no version compatibility checking — if a user has sessions from v1.x, they may not work with v2.x. The web server in web/server.mjs reads its port and host from environment variables, but there's no graceful shutdown mechanism or process manager integration. For robust deployment, the practitioner should use PM2 or systemd to manage the web server process, with automatic restart on crash and log rotation.
7.1.2.strategist: Environment strategy should support the product's growth trajectory. Current state: single environment (local). This is fine for <100 users but becomes a liability at scale. Recommended evolution: (1) Phase 1 (current, <100 users): Single environment, ~/.space/projects/ default, environment variables for overrides. (2) Phase 2 (100-1000 users): Add SPACE_ENV variable, separate dev/prod directories, add staging environment for testing new features. (3) Phase 3 (1000+ users): Multi-tenant support, per-project configuration, environment-aware exports (e.g., dev exports include debug metadata, prod exports are clean). The release management gap is the most critical business risk — without formal versioning and release notes, users can't assess upgrade risk. Solution: adopt semantic versioning strictly, generate release notes automatically from git commits (conventional commits), publish a CHANGELOG.md. For the hosted SaaS version (future), the environment strategy must include: (1) Per-user data isolation, (2) LLM API key management (user-provided or shared), (3) Export quota management, (4) Session timeout and cleanup. The SPACE_PROJECTS_DIR configuration is the foundation — it enables all these scenarios by making storage location configurable.
7.1.2.critic: The environment management is inadequate for anything beyond personal use. (1) No environment separation: dev and prod share ~/.space/projects/, meaning a test run could overwrite a user's real session data. The FileSystemStorage in src/storage/filesystem.ts creates directories in the constructor — running tests that create FileSystemStorage instances writes to the user's actual projects directory. (2) No database migrations: the SQLiteStorage schema (defined in SCHEMA_SQL in src/storage/sqlite.ts) has no version tracking — if the schema changes between versions, existing databases become unreadable. (3) No configuration validation: SpaceConfig accepts any string for llm_provider, but only specific values are valid — an invalid value silently falls through to NullProvider in src/llm/factory.ts. This should fail loudly. (4) The web server has no CORS configuration, no rate limiting, no authentication — it's unsuitable for any environment beyond localhost. (5) No .env file support — the Twelve-Factor App methodology recommends .env files for local development, but SPACE only reads from process.env. (6) The default directory ~/.space/projects/ doesn't differentiate between environments, making backup/restore error-prone. (7) Framework version compatibility is checked at load time (validateFramework in src/data/framework-loader.ts) but not at session resume — a session created with framework v1.0.0 could be resumed with framework v2.0.0 without warning. These gaps are acceptable for a v2.1.0 solo project but must be addressed before public launch.

7.2.1.architect: SPACE's observability architecture leverages the Engine's event system in src/engine/core.ts as a lightweight telemetry backbone. The SpaceInstance.on(event, handler) pattern emits typed events (session:created, answer:submitted, round:completed, etc.) that any subsystem can subscribe to. This is architecturally equivalent to OpenTelemetry's span model — events carry implicit context (session_id, question_id) and can be forwarded to external systems. The Intelligence layer in src/intelligence/ already consumes these events to compute SessionMetrics (completeness scores, time-per-question, series progress). For production observability, the architecture supports three additions: (1) A structured logger that subscribes to engine events and writes JSON-formatted logs (compatible with Datadog, CloudWatch, etc.), (2) Error tracking via try/catch wrappers around StorageProvider and LLMProvider calls, (3) Performance tracing by timestamping event emission and consumption. The CLI's console output (chalk-colored terminal text) is a form of manual observability but isn't structured or machine-parseable. The web server should add request logging middleware. The absence of a health check endpoint beyond GET /api/health (returning { status: 'ok' }) means monitoring can detect server availability but not functional correctness.
7.2.1.practitioner: Current observability: CLI prints to stdout/stderr using chalk for formatting. Web server uses console.log for request logging. The Engine emits events via the on() pattern — handlers are registered by src/intelligence/index.ts to compute metrics. No structured logging library is installed. No metrics collection. No distributed tracing. For adding observability: (1) Structured logging: Install pino (fast JSON logger), create a logger module in src/logging/logger.ts, subscribe to Engine events, emit log entries with session_id, question_id, timestamp, and event_type. (2) Error tracking: Wrap LLM provider calls in src/llm/providers/*.ts with try/catch, log errors with context. (3) Performance: Add timing instrumentation to src/engine/question-router.ts — measure time between getCurrentQuestion() and submitAnswer() to identify slow questions. (4) Health check: Extend the web server's GET /api/health to include database connectivity, LLM provider availability, and storage directory writability. For monitoring: if the web server runs in production, use process.on('uncaughtException') and process.on('unhandledRejection') handlers in web/server.mjs. The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts silently swallows errors (returns empty string on failure) — this should log warnings.
7.2.1.strategist: Observability strategy should match the deployment model. Current (local CLI): minimal logging is correct — the developer IS the user and can observe behavior directly. No need for Sentry, Datadog, or similar tools. The investment should go into self-diagnostic capabilities: 'space doctor' command that checks: (1) Node.js version compatibility, (2) ~/.space/ directory writable, (3) Framework files valid, (4) LLM provider reachable (if configured), (5) Git initialized (if auto-commit enabled). Future (hosted SaaS): observability becomes critical. Minimum requirements: (1) Request logging with correlation IDs, (2) Error tracking (Sentry or equivalent), (3) Usage analytics (Mixpanel or PostHog — track: sessions started, questions answered, exports generated), (4) LLM cost monitoring (track tokens used per session, alert on threshold). Key metrics for the business: (1) Daily active sessions (engagement), (2) Session completion rate (quality), (3) Average time to complete all 326 probes (efficiency), (4) LLM cost per session (unit economics), (5) Export format distribution (user preference). For the CLI tool, 'space stats' command showing personal usage (total sessions, average completion, total time) would add value without requiring external observability infrastructure.
7.2.1.critic: The observability story is the weakest aspect of SPACE's architecture. (1) Zero structured logging means debugging production issues is impossible — there's no log file, no log aggregation, no way to reconstruct what happened. (2) The Engine's event system is not typed — event names are strings, so a typo in 'session:created' vs 'session:creatd' would silently fail. (3) The GitIntegration class (src/integration/git.ts) swallows ALL errors — the run() method catches exceptions and returns empty string, making git failures invisible. This is particularly dangerous for auto-commit: if git commit fails, the user loses version history without knowing. (4) The LLM providers in src/llm/providers/*.ts have inconsistent error handling — OpenAIProvider and AnthropicProvider throw on failure, but the caller in core.ts may not catch these, causing unhandled rejections. (5) The web server has no request ID tracking, no response time logging, no error rate monitoring. (6) FileSystemStorage uses sync I/O, so a slow disk operation blocks the entire process with no visibility into what's slow. (7) There's no audit trail for data modifications — if a session is corrupted, there's no way to determine what changed or when. The event system is a good foundation, but it's underutilized. Without structured logging, SPACE is flying blind in any environment beyond local development.

7.2.2.architect: SPACE's configuration architecture follows the layered configuration pattern defined in src/config/defaults.ts: built-in defaults → environment variables → CLI arguments. The SpaceConfig type is the single source of truth for all configurable parameters, with 16 fields covering storage paths, LLM settings, UI preferences, and export options. This is architecturally clean — there's one type, one default object, one merge point. The configuration is loaded once at createSpace() initialization and immutable thereafter, following the Configuration Object pattern. This design prevents configuration drift but also means runtime changes (like switching LLM providers) require a new SpaceInstance. The feature management approach is implicit: boolean flags in SpaceConfig (enable_adaptive_questions, enable_quality_scoring) act as feature toggles. These are static — set at startup, never changed. For a feature flag system, the architecture would need a FeatureFlags interface that supports runtime evaluation: isEnabled(feature: string, context?: object): boolean. The current approach is simpler and sufficient for the product's maturity. The lack of configuration files (.env, config.json) is a deliberate choice — all config flows through environment variables, which is twelve-factor compliant but limits discoverability. Users can't see what's configured without inspecting process.env.
7.2.2.practitioner: Configuration in practice: SpaceConfig is defined in src/config/defaults.ts with DEFAULT_CONFIG as the baseline. The createSpace() function in src/engine/core.ts merges user-provided partial config with defaults. Environment variable mapping (not currently implemented but implied by the SpaceConfig fields): SPACE_PROJECTS_DIR → config.projects_dir, SPACE_LLM_PROVIDER → config.llm_provider, SPACE_LLM_API_KEY → config.llm_api_key. CLI arguments override env vars (handled by Commander in src/cli/index.ts). Runtime configuration: none — config is frozen after createSpace(). Feature toggles: enable_adaptive_questions controls whether src/intelligence/adaptive-router.ts modifies question flow; enable_quality_scoring controls whether src/llm/quality-scorer.ts evaluates answers. Both are booleans in SpaceConfig, read once at initialization. To add a new feature toggle: (1) Add a boolean field to SpaceConfig interface, (2) Add a default value to DEFAULT_CONFIG, (3) Read the value in the relevant module. No dynamic reload, no A/B testing infrastructure, no gradual rollout mechanism. The web server reads SPACE_PROJECTS_DIR from process.env at startup — this is the only runtime configuration path. For testing different configurations, the practitioner can create multiple SpaceInstance objects with different Partial<SpaceConfig> overrides via createSpace({ llm_provider: 'openai', ... }), enabling side-by-side comparison of different settings during development.
7.2.2.strategist: Configuration strategy should balance simplicity with extensibility. Current: static config via env vars is the right choice for a CLI tool — it's simple, debuggable, and twelve-factor compliant. For the product roadmap: (1) Short term: Document all environment variables in README.md with examples. Add 'space config' command to display current configuration. (2) Medium term: Add .env file support for local development — dotenv library, loaded before env vars. (3) Long term: Add per-project configuration via .space/config.json in the project directory — enables project-specific LLM providers, export formats, and feature toggles. Feature management strategy: current boolean flags (enable_adaptive_questions, enable_quality_scoring) should evolve to a three-tier model: (1) Global defaults in SpaceConfig, (2) Per-project overrides in project config, (3) Per-session overrides for experimentation. This enables A/B testing of features without global deployment. The feature flag approach should NOT be over-engineered — LaunchDarkly-style feature management is overkill for a CLI tool. Simple boolean flags with environment variable overrides are sufficient until there are 1000+ users, at which point graduated rollouts become necessary. Priority: focus on making existing configuration discoverable (documentation, 'space config' command) before adding new configuration mechanisms.
7.2.2.critic: The configuration approach has several blind spots. (1) No configuration validation: SpaceConfig accepts any value for llm_provider, but only 'openai' | 'anthropic' | 'gemini' | 'mistral' | 'ollama' | 'local' | 'none' are valid. An invalid value silently falls through to NullProvider in src/llm/factory.ts — the user thinks LLM is configured but it isn't. This should throw an error at startup. (2) No environment variable mapping: despite the design implication, SpaceConfig doesn't actually read from process.env — the createSpace() function only accepts a Partial<SpaceConfig> parameter. Users must pass config programmatically or via CLI arguments. Environment variables are NOT wired up. (3) No configuration discovery: there's no 'space config --list' command, no documentation of available variables, no config validation command. (4) The enable_adaptive_questions flag is read by the intelligence layer but there's no feedback mechanism — users can't tell if adaptive routing is active during a session. (5) The LLM configuration has no connection testing — if SPACE_LLM_API_KEY is invalid, the error only surfaces during a session, not at startup. (6) No configuration export — users can't share their configuration with teammates or backup their settings. (7) The default export format is 'markdown' but there's no way to change this globally without an environment variable that isn't documented. The configuration system works for the developer who built it but is opaque to everyone else.

7.3.1.architect: SPACE's maintenance architecture is designed for minimal operational overhead through three strategies: (1) Dependency minimization — the package.json lists only 6 runtime dependencies (chalk, commander, inquirer, sql.js, vitest for dev), reducing the attack surface and update burden. (2) Storage abstraction — the StorageProvider interface in src/storage/types.ts allows swapping FileSystemStorage for SQLiteStorage (or a future PostgresStorage) without modifying the engine. This means storage migrations can be handled at the provider level. (3) Framework versioning — the FrameworkDefinition.meta.version field (currently '2.0.0') enables backward compatibility tracking. The engine validates framework versions via validateFramework() in src/data/framework-loader.ts, providing early detection of incompatibilities. Lifecycle management concern: the SQLiteStorage persists data via this.db.export() → writeFileSync() after every mutation — this is not crash-safe. A maintenance task should add WAL mode or checkpoint-based persistence. The GitIntegration class in src/integration/git.ts provides automatic version control for exported specs, which is a built-in backup mechanism. Node.js version support (18, 20, 22 in engines field) aligns with the current LTS releases — maintenance should track the Node.js release schedule and drop EOL versions annually.
7.3.1.practitioner: Maintenance tasks with specific files and commands: (1) Dependency updates: 'npm audit' checks for vulnerabilities, 'npm outdated' lists available updates. Critical dependencies to monitor: sql.js (SQLite WASM), inquirer (CLI prompts), chalk (terminal colors). (2) Node.js compatibility: Test matrix should include Node 18, 20, 22. The engines field in package.json enforces >=18.0.0. (3) TypeScript updates: 'npx tsc --version' — TypeScript 5.x is current. Breaking changes between TS versions can affect strict mode behavior in src/types/index.ts. (4) Framework updates: modify JSON files in prompt-framework/, bump meta.version, add migration logic in src/data/framework-loader.ts if schema changes. (5) Bug fixes: Write a failing test first (in the relevant *.test.ts file), fix the source code, verify test passes. (6) Feature additions: Add TypeScript interfaces first, implement, add tests. Upgrade policy: non-breaking for MINOR/PATCH (per semver). Breaking changes (MAJOR): update FrameworkDefinition schema, add migration tool in src/data/framework-loader.ts, update README with migration guide. No formal deprecation policy — old API surface is removed without notice at this scale.
7.3.1.strategist: Maintenance strategy should be proportional to the user base and revenue. Current (<100 users): Ad-hoc maintenance — fix bugs as reported, update dependencies monthly. This is sustainable for a solo developer. Growth phase (100-1000 users): Introduce a maintenance calendar: (1) Weekly: run 'npm audit', check GitHub issues, (2) Monthly: update dependencies, review open issues, (3) Quarterly: Node.js version support review, major dependency updates, (4) Annually: security audit, architecture review. Revenue-generating maintenance priorities: (1) Bug fixes that affect session completion (direct impact on user value), (2) LLM provider updates when APIs change (direct impact on functionality), (3) Export format improvements (user-facing value), (4) Performance optimization (user experience). Maintenance cost model: ~2 hours/week for a solo developer at <100 users, ~10 hours/week at 1000+ users. The minimal dependency strategy pays off here — fewer dependencies means fewer security patches and compatibility issues. Success metrics: (1) Mean time to fix a critical bug (target: <24 hours), (2) Dependency update lag (target: <30 days for security patches), (3) Breaking change frequency (target: <1 per quarter). The lifecycle should be open-ended — there's no reason to sunset a tool that works well and serves its purpose.
7.3.1.critic: The maintenance plan has significant gaps that will cause problems as the project matures. (1) No automated dependency updates — Dependabot or Renovate should be configured to create PRs for outdated dependencies. Without this, the project will accumulate outdated packages with known vulnerabilities. (2) No security scanning — 'npm audit' is manual, not automated. A GitHub Action should run on every push and block merges on high-severity vulnerabilities. (3) No Node.js version testing matrix — the engines field says >=18 but there's no CI to verify actual compatibility with Node 18, 20, and 22. (4) No framework migration strategy — the framework JSON schema could change between versions, but there's no migration tool or compatibility layer. Existing sessions from v2.0.0 would break with a v3.0.0 schema change. (5) The SQLiteStorage has no backup strategy — a corrupted database file means all session data is lost. (6) No end-of-life policy — what happens if the developer stops maintaining the project? The MIT license allows forks, but without documentation on the architecture and extension points, forking is difficult. (7) The minimal dependency strategy is a double-edged sword — sql.js (SQLite compiled to WASM) is a complex dependency that could have its own breaking changes, and the project has no plan for handling this. Maintenance should include a 'bus factor' assessment: if the developer is unavailable for 6 months, what breaks? The answer: everything, because there's no CI, no documentation, no contributor guide.

7.3.2.architect: SPACE's stewardship architecture is designed for single-developer ownership with community extensibility. The key architectural decisions supporting this: (1) Plugin-ready interfaces — StorageProvider, LLMProvider, and ExportResult are defined as interfaces, not implementations. Community members can add new storage backends, LLM providers, or export formats without modifying core code. (2) Data-driven framework — the 326 probes are in JSON files, not hardcoded. Community members can author new frameworks without touching TypeScript. (3) Event-driven intelligence — the Engine's on/emit pattern allows external tools to observe and react to session events without modifying the engine. However, the current extensibility model has a critical limitation: the switch statements in src/llm/factory.ts and src/export/index.ts require modifying core code to add new providers/exporters. A registry pattern (Map<string, Factory>) would enable drop-in extensibility. The long-term architectural evolution should consider: (1) Splitting the Engine into smaller packages (space-engine, space-storage, space-llm) for independent versioning, (2) Publishing the StorageProvider and LLMProvider interfaces as @space/types for third-party implementors, (3) Adding a plugin manifest system (like VS Code extensions) for runtime extensibility.
7.3.2.practitioner: Stewardship for a practitioner means understanding ownership boundaries and extension points. Currently owned by the original developer: all TypeScript source in src/, framework JSON in prompt-framework/, web UI in web/, CLI in src/cli/. Extension points for community contributors: (1) New LLM providers: implement src/llm/providers/newprovider.ts satisfying the LLMProvider interface (name, complete(), isAvailable()), add a case to createProvider() in src/llm/factory.ts. (2) New export formats: implement src/export/formatters/newformat-exporter.ts returning ExportResult, add a case to exportSession() in src/export/index.ts. (3) New storage backends: implement src/storage/newstorage.ts satisfying StorageProvider, instantiate in createSpace(). (4) New framework probes: add JSON files following FrameworkDefinition schema in prompt-framework/. The MIT license enables forking, but the monolithic structure (single package.json, single tsconfig.json) makes selective forking difficult. For long-term maintenance: track the Node.js LTS release schedule, update engines field annually, test against new LTS versions within 30 days of release. The framework version (2.0.0) should follow its own release cycle independent of the CLI version, with migration tools in src/data/framework-loader.ts.
7.3.2.strategist: Long-term stewardship is the most important strategic decision for the project's future. Three viable models: (1) Solo maintainer (current) — sustainable until the user base exceeds what one person can support (~500 active users). Advantages: singular vision, fast decisions, zero coordination overhead. Risks: bus factor of 1, burnout, knowledge concentration. (2) Build-and-run team (2-3 people) — sustainable for 500-5000 users. The team owns both development and operations. Advantages: redundancy, specialization, faster iteration. Risks: coordination cost, culture alignment, funding requirements. (3) Open-source community — sustainable for 5000+ users. External contributions, governance model, foundation oversight. Advantages: scalability, community innovation, reduced bus factor. Risks: governance complexity, quality control, direction disputes. Recommended path: start with solo (current), transition to build-and-run at $10K MRR, consider open-source governance at $50K MRR or 1000 GitHub stars. The open-source community model requires significant investment: CONTRIBUTING.md, code of conduct, governance document, maintainer guidelines, release process documentation. This investment is justified only when community contributions are consistently >30% of total changes. Success metrics for stewardship: (1) Continuity — no gaps in maintenance longer than 2 weeks, (2) Responsiveness — issue response time <48 hours, (3) Knowledge transfer — any TypeScript developer can become productive in the codebase within 1 week.
7.3.2.critic: The stewardship plan has a critical vulnerability: bus factor of one. If the original developer becomes unavailable, the project has: (1) No documented architecture beyond code comments, (2) No contributor guide, (3) No governance model, (4) No release automation, (5) No issue triage process. The 'any competent TypeScript developer could take over' claim is dangerously optimistic — the codebase has undocumented design decisions (why SQLite over Postgres? why sync I/O? why no ESLint?), implicit assumptions (the framework JSON format, the artifact dictionary schema), and tribal knowledge (which tests are important, which modules are fragile) that would take weeks to transfer. The succession plan should include: (1) Architecture documentation (ADRs for major decisions), (2) A 'runbook' for common maintenance tasks, (3) A designated successor with repository write access and deployment credentials, (4) Automated CI/CD so maintenance can continue without the original developer's local environment. The open-source aspiration (MIT license, community contributions welcome) conflicts with the reality (no CONTRIBUTING.md, no issue templates, no PR review process). The project is technically open-source but practically closed — only the original developer can effectively contribute. Long-term stewardship requires either: (a) investing in community infrastructure now, or (b) honestly positioning the project as 'maintained by [name]' with no community expectations. The worst outcome is promising community governance without delivering it.
